newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila markets mixed as Thai fears ebb.
newsitem.headline: Manila markets mixed as Thai fears ebb.

text.p: Philippine markets were mixed on Thursday as analysts said fears over the de facto devaluation of the Thai baht were dying.
Central Bank governor Gabriel Singson said the monetary authority had turned into a buyer of dollars in morning deals after its heavy dollar selling yesterday to protect the peso.
"Things have settled," Singson told reporters, adding that the bank bought about $45 million in morning deals.
The Philippine stock market, however, shed 22.47 points to finish at 2,742.42 points.
"The market is driven by sentiment on the Thai baht crisis but this should not call for much worry," said Dharmala Securities economist Manuel Goseco.
"I advise a hold on stocks, but interest in the equities market will pick up as soon as we get the Thai issue out of the way, which should happen in a couple of days," he said.
"The money will be going out of the stock market in the near term to take advantage of higher interest rates," said Jose Ricardo Garcia, executive vice president of Diversified Securities.
On Wednesday, the Philippine Central Bank lifted its key overnight borrowing rate by nine percentage points to 24 percent and sold a heavy amount of dollars.
In recent months, investors had been drawing parallels between Thailand and the Philippines since both have a current account deficit and an overheated property sector.
Volume in the currency market was still light at mid-day at around $250 million, compared to about $800 million done by this time on Wednesday. The day's turnover was a record $1.05 billion.
The peso was trading in the range of 26.41/26.403 compared to the closing of 26.376.
Traders said the peso was pulled down, not by concerns driven by the Thai baht but on arbitrage play for the long weekend that takes into account the New York holiday on Friday, traders said.
Singson said the Central Bank's emergency measure to protect the peso was temporary and would not affect business activities.
"As speculation stops, we will start pulling down the rate. These are only temporary and the businessmen know," he said.
